claims.text: A hybrid MTP–thermodynamic-integration framework can accurately predict melting temperature, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity across vast HEA compositional spaces.
The hybrid framework overcomes the limitations of standard DFT and classical potentials at extreme temperatures.
The target alloys are substitutional solid solutions with severe local lattice distortion and high configurational entropy.
MTPs can be trained on DFT energies and forces from representative HEA configurations.
MTP-assisted molecular dynamics and thermodynamic integration can determine the solid and liquid Gibbs free energies as functions of temperature.
The free-energy crossing gives the melting temperature, while temperature derivatives provide entropy of fusion and heat capacity.
The method is applicable from cryogenic temperatures to above 1500 K, near ambient pressure, and to alloys containing 4–10 principal elements.
Adequate DFT training data are required to capture the diverse local environments of HEAs.
MTPs capture HEA many-body interactions and local distortions with near-DFT accuracy.
MTPs operate at a cost comparable to classical potentials and enable the large-scale sampling required for thermodynamic integration.
Standard DFT is too computationally expensive to provide the extensive sampling needed for converged free energies in multicomponent alloys.
Classical EAM and MEAM potentials often fail to represent the electronic and chemical interactions needed for accurate HEA melting predictions.
The expressivity of MTPs allows them to learn a DFT-quality potential-energy surface and bridge the accuracy–cost gap.
Thermodynamic integration with the learned potential directly yields melting properties without empirical rules or experimental fitting.
The framework will predict HEA melting temperatures within 50–100 K of experiment.
The framework will provide reliable entropy-of-fusion and heat-capacity estimates where experimental data are sparse or unreliable.
The framework will enable high-throughput screening at a computational cost 4–10 times lower than pure DFT.
Empirical rules and small-supercell DFT calculations often fail because they omit HEA configurational complexity and anharmonicity.
The method is valid primarily for substitutional solid-solution HEAs and may struggle with strong chemical ordering, intermetallic formation, or amorphous structures.

Accuracy is limited by training-set size and diversity, extrapolation into unexplored compositions, and finite-time convergence of thermodynamic integration, with larger uncertainty for complex phase behavior.
